iTerm2 is a replacement for Terminal and the successor to iTerm. It works on Macs with macOS 10.14 or newer.
Objecting to the new AI feature in iTerm2, one user said it takes much less effort to simply switch back to Terminal.app than to edit the feature out.
A user who generally hates 'shoved-down-your-throat' AI said they weren't bothered by iTerm2's AI feature because it's totally optional and unobtrusive.
The AI feature isn't enabled by default and requires your own API key, so the app is the same for anyone who doesn't want it.
Workaround for wanting local models: the OpenAI URL is configurable under Advanced > Experimental > URL for AI API, and Ollama offers OpenAI-compatible endpoints, so this may already work.

One user prompted the iTerm2 AI feature to use awk to filter the 2nd and 5th columns of piped input and truncate the 5th to 25 chars. They said it was about 10x faster than a Google search or man page, and they verify results by checking the output.
'It was very jarring to open up my terminal one day and be greeted by yEt AnOtHeR gReAt Ai FeAtUrE.' The user thinks the onboarding screens fueled the backlash.
A user was warned that iTerm2 sent all terminal interactions to OpenAI even without an API key. The packet captures offered as proof were made with an invalid key, not a blank one.
Complaint: the AI feature is 'unconfigured', not disabled. Any value in the API key field, even an accidental space, activates it. The user wanted a real, clear toggle to turn the function off.
Rebuttal: even with a key entered, nothing is sent until you open the new Codecierge toolbox and type in a question.

Criticism that an iTerm2 vulnerability was publicly disclosed only 18 days after being reported, before the fix reached stable releases. The blog post contained far more detail than the upstream commit.

The blog post author said they built an exploit just by prompting an LLM with the upstream iTerm2 commit. They said the iTerm2 author initially didn't consider the bug severe enough for an immediate release but later reconsidered.
Workaround for escape-sequence attacks: alias cat to 'strings -a --unicode=hex' so the terminal doesn't interpret hidden characters in files.

Praise for imgcat, which shows images without leaving the terminal and works across SSH. Also for the Python scripting API: 'basically AppleScript for iTerm' but not soul-crushing to write. The user's script switches themes with the system appearance.
A user who got 'imgcat: command not found' was told it isn't installed by default: download it from iterm2.com/utilities/imgcat and put it on your PATH.

'imgcat and image displaying is amazing.' One user uses a matplotlib backend that renders plots inline, which makes remote work nicer. it2dl downloads files from the remote system browser-style and is much more convenient than scp when several sessions deep.

One user felt the image extensions were 'almost there' but limited to displaying files rather than images generated on the fly. Another replied that the protocol supports it if you prepend the escape sequence to base64 data.

A non-Mac user said they're 'a little jealous of iTerm'; the UX is nice and they can't find a like-for-like replacement on Windows or Linux. Another said it's something they miss a great deal on other OSes.
Semantic History is handy and little known: Command+Click a path to open it in your editor, or Command+Drag a path into other apps' file dropzones.
Caution on Semantic History: 'it's not shy about creating invalid file references when it doesn't know what it's talking about.'
A user wrote iterm2-dwim to extract paths and line numbers from formats iTerm2 didn't handle, such as Python and pdb stack traces and git diff 'a/b' prefixes.
